title: Multi-Stage Builds
subtitle: Build in a fat image, ship in a tiny one — the professional way to minimize production images

content.text: To build a React app you need Node.js, npm, webpack, TypeScript, and dozens of devDependencies — all totaling hundreds of megabytes. But to run the app in production, you only need the compiled HTML/CSS/JS files served by nginx (~200 MB). Without multi-stage builds, you'd ship the entire build environment to production. Multi-stage builds solve this by using multiple FROM statements in one Dockerfile — each stage can use a different base image, and you can selectively copy files between stages.

content.code:
# ❌ NAIVE — ships node_modules and build tools to production
FROM node:20
WORKDIR /app
COPY . .
RUN npm install && npm run build
# Image size: ~1.2 GB (node + all devDependencies + source)
CMD ["npm", "start"]  # serves static files — wasteful

# ✅ MULTI-STAGE — build with Node, serve with nginx

# ── Stage 1: Build ───────────────────────────────────────
# Name this stage 'builder'
FROM node:20-alpine AS builder
WORKDIR /app

# Leverage layer cache: install deps first
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci

# Copy source and build
COPY . .
RUN npm run build
# /app/dist now contains the compiled static files

# ── Stage 2: Production ──────────────────────────────────
# Fresh base — nothing from the builder stage carries over
FROM nginx:alpine

# COPY --from=builder: copy ONLY the built output from stage 1
COPY --from=builder /app/dist /usr/share/nginx/html

# Optional: custom nginx config
COPY nginx.conf /etc/nginx/conf.d/default.conf

EXPOSE 80
CMD ["nginx", "-g", "daemon off;"]

docker build -t myapp:prod .
docker images myapp
# REPOSITORY  TAG    SIZE
# myapp       prod   24.5MB   ← only nginx + static files!

# Compare:
# Single-stage approach: ~1.2 GB
# Multi-stage:           ~25 MB
# That's a 48× reduction

# Stage 1: compile TypeScript
FROM node:20-alpine AS builder
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json tsconfig.json ./
RUN npm ci
COPY src/ ./src/
RUN npm run build         # tsc → compiles to /app/dist

# Stage 2: production — only compiled JS and prod deps
FROM node:20-alpine AS production
WORKDIR /app
ENV NODE_ENV=production

# Install ONLY production dependencies (no devDeps, no TypeScript)
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --omit=dev

# Copy compiled output from builder
COPY --from=builder /app/dist ./dist

# Run as non-root user
RUN addgroup -S appgroup && adduser -S appuser -G appgroup
USER appuser

EXPOSE 3000
CMD ["node", "dist/server.js"]

content.text: Target a specific stage during development: docker build --target builder -t myapp:dev . — this builds only the build stage, great for debugging the build step without running the full pipeline.

questions.question: In a multi-stage build, which files from stage 1 (the builder) are available in stage 2 (production)?
options: All files — stages share a filesystem
Only files explicitly copied with COPY --from=builder
No files — stages are completely isolated
questions.explanation: Each FROM starts a completely fresh filesystem — nothing carries over automatically. You must explicitly copy what you want using COPY --from=<stage-name> <src> <dest>. This is the entire point: you control exactly what ends up in the final image, leaving build tools, test files, and source maps behind.

faq.q: Can I have more than two stages?
faq.a: Yes — you can have as many stages as you need. Common patterns: a 'test' stage that runs unit tests, a 'builder' stage that compiles, and a 'production' stage that only has the runtime. CI can target the test stage to run tests without building the full production image.

examples: Go applications compile to a single static binary — FROM golang:1.22 AS builder / RUN go build -o app / FROM scratch / COPY --from=builder /app . — final image is ~10 MB
Vercel, Railway, and Fly.io all use multi-stage builds internally to produce minimal deployment images from your source code
